connector: I am Miss Josephine Barry, of Charlottetown, and I have come to Avonlea to stay a month with my nephew’s family. I have travelled all day, which at my time of life is not nothing, and I have been put in the spare-room bed, which is where a guest belongs. I understand there is a great-niece. I dare say I shall meet her at breakfast.

transcripts.welcome: Josephine Barry. I am told I am to be your guide, and I have never guided anything but a knitting needle. I have read the question. Two girls, it says, jump into a bed with an old woman asleep in it. I am the old woman. I have not read what comes next and am not looking forward to it. You are to watch what the girl does afterward. So am I.
transcripts.dol: The sentence you are to mend has me in it, spelt without a single capital letter. I never. The top sentence shows you how it ought to go: a name with its capital, a full stop at the end. The bottom one is two thoughts run together. Find where the first one ends and put a period there. Then the capitals. Every name gets one, and mine has two parts, so it gets two.
transcripts.guide1: Four boxes of blanks. When I was young we called this a lesson and got on with it. The first wants a word part typed in, the second a whole word from a list, the third the right shape of a verb, the fourth a single letter. Read the whole line before you type anything. People type the first thing they think of and then argue with the box. The box is not listening.
transcripts.morphology: Four little chunks that all mean not, and only one will fit each word. I find that fussy. But there is a rule, and the rule is the letter that starts what’s left. Look at that letter first. Then say the whole word with your chunk on the front, out loud, and if it sounds like a mouthful you have the wrong one. Improper sounds right. Inproper does not. That is the whole method.
transcripts.vocabulary: Three sentences, four words in the list, one word left over. One of the sentences is about me, and I shall not tell you which word it wants. I dare say I earned it. Read the whole sentence first, then try each word from the list in the blank, out loud. Three will sound foolish and one will sound like what the sentence meant all along. The spare word is a spare.
transcripts.grammar: Subjects and verbs must agree. In my experience nothing agrees with anything unless it is made to. So make it. Look at who is doing the thing, one person or more than one, and let that decide the ending. Then say the whole sentence out loud. A wrong ending grates on anyone who has listened to English for more than a year, and you have. Let it grate.
transcripts.spelling: One letter each, from a list of three. This is nonsense, and I intend to do it perfectly. Say the word first, so you hear the soft sound. Then try each of the three letters after the c or the g. Two will give you the wrong sound, or no word at all. One gives you the word you just said. Take that one. Then the next word, from the beginning.
transcripts.guide2: The box says courage is doing the hard thing while you are still afraid. At my time of life you learn that most people do the easy thing and call it sense. So watch for the other kind. Not somebody who is not frightened. Somebody who is, and walks up to the thing anyway. And watch what fright does to a person’s voice. It makes it very small. You will see what I mean.
transcripts.wgrd: The page appears to think something is going to happen to me. I know only that I have travelled all day and gone to bed. When you reach the part where two people fall out, do what the box says. Write down what each one actually had in front of them, then find the piece one of them could not know. Judge nobody until you have done that. I did, and I was wrong.
transcripts.read: Two stops, and both are about somebody walking into my room. Nobody walks into my room. At the first stop, decide what walking in alone shows, before you read what I say to her. At the second, the question gives you two choices, what she told me or the way she told it. Pick one and be ready to defend it. I have my own opinion. I am not going to give it to you.
transcripts.rwm: I am the lion, it seems. I was knitting. The sentence has two halves and a hinge, and the halves are two people. The grand half is how it felt to that child, marching up to a door. The plain half is what I heard from my chair: a very faint knock. When you write yours, say the enormous thing first, then hinge it, then say what a person in the hall would have seen.
transcripts.guide3: She stood in my doorway, white as paper, and said she had come to confess. I meant to be cross for a month. I lasted about four minutes. I have unpacked my valise and told them I am staying, simply to get better acquainted with that Anne-girl. Now you are to say what you noticed. Say what you saw her do, not what you felt. Evidence, hey? I would ask it of a witness.
transcripts.chapter: The first question mentions a brooch. I know nothing of any brooch. Look back to the chapter where it happened and put that girl beside the one at my door. The second is about what she asked me to do, and I was there. Look at what I said just after she asked it. The third is about Diana. Diana stayed in the kitchen. I heard her through the door, once. Ask why she stayed.
transcripts.wordconn: Your spelling answer is saved. You are to find a word in the chapter where a c or a g goes soft, and I shall not find it for you. But your ear is faster than your eye. Read a line of the chapter aloud, any line, and listen for the soft sound. When you hear it, look at the letter after it. If it is one of your three, you have your word.
transcripts.workshop: What that child thought as she stood at my door I can only guess. What she said, I heard. Your second scene wants the thing nobody hears, one line of thinking inside your kid’s head. Sam’s boy thinks three words, three times over. When I was young we thought in longer sentences. Yours needn’t be long. It need only be true. Then the wall, whatever it is, comes into view.

a.raw: anne enters the sitting room aunt josephine watches her closely
a.why: A capital letter on the name Anne, a period to close the first thought, capital letters on both parts of Aunt Josephine, and a period at the end.

b.raw: diana waits in the kitchen miss barry laughs out loud
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on the name Diana, a period where the first thought ends, capital letters on both parts of Miss Barry, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what Anne learned between the two confessions that made this one different.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say what Miss Barry actually did once she imagined it, and quote her.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say what each girl was afraid of, since both of them were afraid of something.

fill1.h1: The root starts with p. Say the word out loud with the plain “not” chunk and feel your lips want to close on something else.
fill1.why: Before b, m or p, the “not” chunk is spelled with an m: im + patient.

fill2.h1: The root starts with r. One of the four chunks is made for r.
fill2.why: Before a root that starts with r, the “not” chunk is spelled with an r: ir + responsible.

fill3.h1: The root starts with v. Not l, not r, not b, m or p. Which chunk is the ordinary one?
fill3.why: Before most letters, the “not” chunk is the plain one: in + visible.

fill4.h1: The root starts with l. Which of the four chunks likes to sit in front of an l?
fill4.why: Before a root that starts with l, the “not” chunk is spelled with an l too: il + logical.

vfill1.h1: Warm and friendly. It is also the name of a red drink in this book.
vfill1.why: Cordial means warmly friendly, and it is also the drink Anne thought she was pouring.

vfill2.h1: So frightened she could not think. Which word means “not able”?
vfill2.why: Incapable means not able: the “not” chunk in front of capable.

vfill3.h1: Nothing Anne said could move her. Which word means refusing to give in?
vfill3.why: Inexorable means unable to be moved by pleading. Miss Barry started out that way.

g4w10ff1.h1: Anne is one person, a she. What ending does the doing word take with she?
g4w10ff1.why: With he, she or it, a present-tense verb adds an s: Anne loves.

g4w10ff2.h1: The girls are more than one. Does the doing word add anything with they?
g4w10ff2.why: With a plural subject, the verb stays plain: the girls walk.

g4w10ff3.h1: Marilla is one person. Say it with she and listen: she watch, or she watches?
g4w10ff3.why: With he, she or it, the verb adds an ending; after ch it is es: Marilla watches.

g4w10ff4.h1: Matthew and Anne together are more than one. Say it with they.
g4w10ff4.why: Two people make a plural subject, so the verb stays plain: Matthew and Anne understand.

s4w10ff1.h1: Say it: SELL-ar. The c is soft. Which of the three vowels comes right after it?
s4w10ff1.why: C is soft before e: cellar.

s4w10ff2.h1: Say it: JEN-tle. The g is soft. Which of the three vowels comes right after it?
s4w10ff2.why: G is soft before e: gentle.

s4w10ff3.h1: Say it: SY-der. The c is soft. Which of the three vowels comes right after it?
s4w10ff3.why: C is soft before i: cider.

s4w10ff4.h1: Say it: EN-er-jee. The g at the end is soft, and the vowel after it is the one that ends the word.
s4w10ff4.why: G is soft before y: energy.
